turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): I've popped Mrs Hale's numbers on the screen. Pressure's 138 over 82, heart rate 76, temperature 36.6, and sats are 97 percent on room air. She's been asking a lot of questions out in the waiting room.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ta. Your daughter can stay, Mrs Hale. It's the six-week check after the right hip replacement, yes?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, six weeks. I came in because the hip still doesn't feel like mine and I need someone to tell me if that's normal. I'm a bit worked up, sorry.
[SEG0004] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She's had a list of questions since breakfast. I'm Kate, her daughter, and I've been staying most nights since the op to look after her.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Kate, let me talk. Um, I'm still on the stick inside and out, is that too long, what if it pops out? I read something online and—

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll get to that. On the couch first. The right hip wound's healed, closed and dry, no redness and no ooze, and you're walking with the stick with a mild limp, which is what I'd expect at six weeks.

[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh, ok. It aches deep in the right side, mostly when I've been up, and the Panadol takes the edge off, two of the 500 milligram ones four times a day, plus the little asprin, 100 milligrams, every morning for the clots. Do I have to keep both, and if I forget a dose does a clot just form?

[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): So that's aspirin 100 milligrams each morning for clots, and paracetamol one gram four times a day for the ache. Missing one aspirin doesn't mean a clot appears. Any swelling of the calf, either side?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No swelling, I've been looking every night. Would it be hot as well, and red? Should Kate be checking too?
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): A clot can make the calf swollen, sometimes warm. Yours isn't. Have you had any fevers?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No fevers, I check with a thermometer. Can I have a bath yet, or only showers? The scar feels tight, are the stitches still in there?
[SEG0012] person_1 (NURSE): Those dissolvable stitches are long gone, love, you won't see them. I can grab the postop sheet after, if you want it.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Showers are fine, and a bath once you can get out safely with Kate nearby. Any cough?
[SEG0014] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, the car park was a shocker. Go on, Mum.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No cough, none at all. I was only clearing my throat outside. That isn't a cough, is it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, throat clearing isn't a cough. And your weight, has it shifted since the operation?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really. I haven't been on the scales. Does weight affect the new joint, should I be dieting, I don't want to mess the hip up?
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing you've said makes me chase your weight today. Last of the general questions. Any problems with your bowels or with passing urine?

[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No, both are normal, same as before the op. Why do you ask, is there a nerve that gets damaged? I read about foot drop and now I'm scared, my foot's not dropping, I don't think, is it?
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Foot drop would mean you couldn't lift the foot, and you just did. No foot drop. Bowels and bladder as they were, that's good.

[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Right, thank god. Um, my father had diabetes in his fifties, Mum did not, my other sister has the pressure but no sugar, and there's a brother who, actually I don't know, we don't talk. Does diabetes in the family mean the hip won't heal?

[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): So your father had diabetes, your sister has high blood pressure, your mother did not have diabetes, and I won't record your brother. It doesn't change how the hip heals. What about day to day, the work, the hours, food, exercise, a drink?

[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): I do the books for the newsagent on the corner, about fifteen hours a week, from the kitchen table. I eat pretty plain, meat and three veg most nights, I was walking the dog every morning before this hip but I can't yet, and I'll have a glass of red with my tea, the evening meal, and I don't smoke. Is fifteen hours too much sitting, should I stand up every—
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every half hour, yes, if you can. Fifteen hours at the table is alright if you get up and move. The dog can wait until you're steadier off the stick.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Righto. Is red wine bad with the asprin, I don't want a stomach bleed? My neighbour had one and I keep thinking about it.

[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): One glass with food is reasonable on low-dose aspirin, and take the tablet with something in your stomach. Black stools or vomiting blood, that's when we worry, not from one glass.

[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Black stools, ok, I'll watch for that. How long do I stay on the asprin, and when can I drive, it's the right hip so it's the pedals? Kate's been driving and she's sick of it.
[SEG0028] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm not sick of it, I'm sick of the parking at this place. I'll keep driving until he says otherwise. Stop putting words in my mouth.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right hip, I'd hold off driving for another fortnight, until you can stamp the brake without thinking. Keep the aspirin going until twelve weeks from the operation, then stop, as long as there's no bleeding. That's the plan I use.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Twelve weeks, so err, six more weeks of it. What about flying to my sister in Brisbane, it's two hours at Christmas? If I get a clot on the plane I'll—

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): A two-hour flight at this stage is generally fine if you're walking and the calf stays quiet. Aisle seat, up every hour, stay on the aspirin. I wouldn't book a long-haul yet.

[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Aisle seat, ok. Is the ache forever, some days a three out of ten, some days a five when I've done the corridor twice? At night it's better if I lie on the other side, is that allowed?

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pain around three to five out of ten, worse after a walk, easier lying on the other side, and the Panadol helps. That pattern fits a hip that's still settling, not one that's infected or come loose. I'd call it a straightforward recovery so far, provisionally.

[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Provisionally, that word worries me. What would infection look like, would I have a fever, you already said I don't? Do I need bloods or an x-ray, I want an x-ray, please?

[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Infection would usually bring a fever, a hot red wound, or feeling properly unwell, and you've not got those. I was going to book the hip x-ray anyway, it's routine at six weeks. No bloods today, the wound isn't angry so they wouldn't change anything.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): No bloods, ok. If the wound gets hot and red I come straight back, yeah, same day, and who do I ring? I'm going to write it down and I'll still forget, I know I will.
[SEG0037] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll write it. If it's hot or red, or the calf swells, we don't wait, we come in. That's what you mean, isn't it?
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, same day, these rooms, or the emergency department if it's after hours. Don't sit on a swollen calf or a wound that's opening.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): After hours, emergency, got it. The physio said one stick, not the frame, and I haven't touched the frame in weeks, is one enough? I don't want to rush it and fall.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): One stick is enough, held in the left hand, opposite the new hip. Wean off it when the limp's gone, there's no rush. I'll see you again in six weeks to go through that x-ray.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Will you have the result by then, and what if it's bad and nobody rings me? I'll ring you myself, I'll be annoying, I know it.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): The report comes to me, and if something needs acting on sooner I'll ring you. Otherwise we go through it at that visit. You won't be annoying.
[SEG0043] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the hip x-ray on the way out, radiology can fit you this afternoon. And I'll put the six-week review in the book. You've still got the stick with you, good.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): This afternoon's good, I want it done. Kate, don't let me leave without the card. If the x-ray's normal I can stop worrying, right, or not really?

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): A normal film is reassuring, it doesn't switch the worry off on its own, but it fits what I'm seeing today. The wound's settled, keep the stick and the aspirin as we said. We'll pick it up in six weeks.

spec.situation: Older patient six weeks after a hip replacement with a daughter; wound healed; walks with a stick; takes aspirin for clots and painkiller; swelling of the calf asked about and denied.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

omissions.text: Negative finding: no foot drop / able to lift the foot.
Negative finding: bowels and bladder normal, same as before the operation, recorded in ROS but not as the specific denied symptoms/problems that were asked and answered.
Negative finding/exam context: calf was not warm; doctor said a clot can make the calf warm and 'Yours isn't.'
Assessment detail missing from exam: gait with stick and mild limp was described as what the doctor would expect at six weeks.
Planned investigation detail: no blood tests today because the wound is not angry and bloods would not change management.
Follow-up/result plan detail: x-ray report will come to the doctor; if something needs acting on sooner the doctor will ring, otherwise it will be reviewed at the six-week visit.
